title: First Homily on the Day of the Dormition

sections.heading: Two truths from the tomb of the Mother of God

pairs.en: One would think that if it were possible and fitting for anyone not to die — like Enoch and Elijah — it would be for the Mother of the Son of God. And yet she fell asleep in the sleep of death! Therefore death is inescapable! On the other hand, if there were in death any real evil for man, then she of all people, the Mother of the Son of God, would not have been subjected to that evil; and yet she underwent death. Therefore death is not an evil, and does no harm to man!
Death is inescapable; death is harmless: these are the two truths that come to mind of their own accord on the day of the Dormition of the Mother of God.

Does a man need to keep them in mind? He needs it urgently. For if death is inescapable, then everyone must prepare for it in good time. And if death in itself is harmless, then there is no reason to fear it and tremble before it.

sections.heading: We live as if we would never die

pairs.en: But do we in fact remember these truths? On the contrary, it seems nothing is so easily forgotten as they are. We live as though we would never die, for we make no preparation whatever for death; and we die as though we would never rise again, for we fear death beyond all measure.

We think little about our death — show me the man who devotes even a few minutes to it each day; and yet death can come to us not only any day, but any minute. Still less do we prepare for death — point out to me where this preparation is, and what it consists of. Is this preparation for death: to hunger after reward upon reward, to raise building upon building, to pass from pleasures and amusements to new pleasures and amusements? You have lived, say, more than half a century; you yourself feel that noon is long past, evening is near, night is in sight — tell me, then, what have you prepared for your lodging underground? And such inattention to death is found in the very oldest among us. What, then, shall we say of men in their prime? What shall we say of the young? You would bring a smile to their lips by reminding them of the need to prepare for death — and yet how many young people go down into the grave every year!

After this one might suppose that we consider any preparation for death entirely unnecessary. But how can it be considered unnecessary? Setting out even on a short journey, we take care what to bring with us, where to lodge, what to occupy ourselves with; yet entering the gates of eternity, we imagine that it makes no difference how we enter them, what we take with us, or in what state we present ourselves! Can there be a greater carelessness toward oneself and one's eternal destiny?

Or is it that we do not love ourselves, and are therefore resigned to whatever may happen to us after death? But there is no such self-hatred in us; we live precisely to please ourselves — we labour to drive away the least sorrow of the soul, and to heal the least sore of the body.
Sorrow and sickness concern us — but death does not, and eternity does not! Incomprehensible blindness! Utter mercilessness toward ourselves!

One explanation alone might be supposed: that we consider death the end of everything — in which case there would be nothing to prepare for and nothing in the future to care about. But we have not sunk to that depth of impiety: we look for the life everlasting; we believe in the resurrection of the dead. We look for it — and do not prepare for that life; we believe — and make no effort to attain the resurrection unto life. We hope and we believe — and we live like sheep for the slaughter! Can anything be more ruinous or more senseless?

It is not hard to guess, however, what brings death into oblivion for us and keeps us from preparing for it. We are too devoted to the life of the flesh and its vanities; and the nature of worldly vanities is such that, like dust on the road, they blind the eyes and do not let us see what lies ahead. Standing in the middle of this cloud — at times a whirlwind — of dust, we are unable to stretch our gaze into the future; we look only around ourselves and are led by the present. When, for instance, is the ambitious man to think of death, if vainglory has so blinded him that all his thoughts and his whole soul are fixed on some coveted reward and distinction? It is enough for him to think and think again how to keep anyone from overtaking him on the way, how to humble a rival, how to draw level with those above him, how to display his merits, conceal his failings, and flatter a powerful superior. When is the rich man to think of death — or the man just beginning to grow rich? His whole mind is already taken up with accounts and calculations: goods sent off here, goods expected from there; a steward unreliable in one place, business itself going badly in another; how to sustain or repair his credit; whether there is an opening to lend money at interest or borrow it. To think all this through, not only his days but his very nights do not suffice. When is the scholar to think of death? He has not yet learned everything, has not yet doubted everything; there is this or that discovery still to be made, this or that suspicion to be raised, predecessors to be surpassed, the attention of contemporaries to be attracted — he may yet be hailed as the luminary of his age and make his name immortal.

So vanity, in its various forms, blinds the eyes! And who is free from this blindness? On the other hand, the image of death is so dreadful that it is frightening even to think of it. One might manage it, perhaps, once a year — in Great Lent, in Holy Week, on Great Friday... At any other time it would mean upsetting one's thoughts for at least a whole week, halting one's affairs, perhaps even damaging one's health. How could one bring oneself to it before the doctor says there is no longer any hope, before the confessor appears with prayer book and cross, before the final illness has grown to its final degree? Then we shall think about it; but until then, why needlessly trouble and disturb ourselves with phantoms?

sections.heading: The first lesson: remember death and prepare for it

pairs.en: Is this not, my brethren, the history of our life? Is this not the pattern of our conduct? Tell me: where in all this is reason, where is calculation, where is love for ourselves? If the enemy who seeks our eternal ruin had been given charge of directing our actions, could he destroy us more surely?

Let us come to our senses, then — whoever can — and shake off this negligence!.. Death is inescapable. Therefore let us keep it always in remembrance; remembering it, let us prepare ourselves for it; and preparing, let us not allow ourselves to be blinded by passing goods and amusements.
This is the first lesson from the tomb of the Mother of God; let us now turn our ears and our attention to the second.

sections.heading: The second lesson: death in itself is not an evil

pairs.en: Her Dormition teaches us that death is inescapable; but at the same time it shows that death, in itself, is not an evil for man. For if it were an evil, then for that very reason the Mother of the Son of God would have been exempted from the necessity of dying. Her example, therefore, ought to serve as a consolation to us all and lift us above the fear of death and the grave. And yet we look upon death as the greatest of evils; we fear the grave as we fear nothing else in the world. What sobbing and tears there are at it, what wailing and fainting! What murmuring and despair! Some cannot even bear the death of those close to them, and follow them into the grave.

Is this how a Christian ought to look upon death? It is true that death is the sorrowful tribute paid to sin, the consequence of our calamitous fall in Eden; but by the grace of Christ this punishment has been turned into a means of our reward. Now, for the true Christian, death is not loss but gain: leaving this vain world that lies in evil, we pass out of it into a higher and better world; casting off the frail covering of the body, we go to be clothed in a new garment, incorruptible and glorified; parting for a little while from our dear ones who remain here, we enter the circle of those dear to us who have departed before us — and, what is more, the closest fellowship of the Angels and of our Lord and Saviour Himself.

What is there here to fear? What is there to lament? Yet we tremble, we sob, we give ourselves over to despair. Why? Because we have never entered into the truths of the Gospel as we ought, and are strangers to the light with which it illumines for us the world beyond the grave; because we are too attached to what is earthly and perishable; because we have never prepared for death. For all these reasons death inevitably appears to us an extreme evil — whereas, given the right disposition of our spirit and heart, given a Christian way of thinking and acting, it could serve us, as it has served all true Christians, even as a comfort and a consolation.

Let us cease, then, to be like senseless children. Let us take from the tomb of the Mother of God this lesson: not to count death, in itself, an evil — for if it becomes one, it is by our own fault, that is, when we depart this life burdened with sins, without true repentance and faith. And with such a way of living, life itself is an even greater evil than death; for death at least puts an end to the unbroken chain of those sins and iniquities on which the life was spent. Amen.
